original_summary: Quadrille is an 18th-century four-player trick-taking game with a 40-card pack and three permanent top trumps: Spadille, Manille and Baste. An auction decides the Taker, who names trump and either calls a King, whose holder becomes a concealed partner, or plays solo against three; the side must take the majority of the ten tricks.

review.evidence: In the reviewed variation, Petite Quadrille II, no simple policy is safe. Always-pass makes a player a perpetual defender who only scores when others fail. Always-bid-5 fails most contracts at the highest stake (v=3). Always-Assist never takes the high solo payoffs. Priority rotates evenly, two hands per seat. With four players and the highest total winning, one rival's loss is not automatically your gain, so the two-player difference trap does not apply.
Bidding to the strength of a 5-card hand, choosing trump and partner, following suit, and counting the 20 cards all reward skill. Over 8 hands, deal luck is diluted but not removed.
Inferring the partner from play, managing the top trumps, and judging when solo pays leave room to improve. A weak player still scores as a defender when Takers overreach.

Hands and partner identity are hidden. Players must infer holdings from bids and the cards played, and plan five tricks ahead. With all 20 cards dealt, perfect counting is possible late in a hand, so the hidden information thins out quickly.
Trick winners, contracts and scores are arithmetic on card codes and counters. No judge is needed.

Position-1 rounds had six choice steps (bid, declare, lead and three follows) against a limit of 4. Rule 12 said the trump suit was both unrevealed and announced, which makes the follow-suit offers unusable.

problems: Choice steps exceed the limit: the auction and declaration share a round with a full trick, giving 6 choice steps where at most 4 are allowed.
Rule 12 contradicts itself: trump is said to be both hidden and announced, so defenders cannot know which cards are trumps and following suit becomes unplayable.
Moving the auction into its own round with 5 tricks per hand would allow only 4 hands in 40 rounds (6 rounds each). That gives one priority per seat and much more deal luck.
With all 20 cards dealt, the hidden state collapses fast: by trick 3 a careful counter knows every hand, so late-hand inference is thin.
The partner is chosen by seat number, which loses the original's characteristic called King. It also lets the Taker pick a partner without any uncertainty about whether that partner is strong.

changes.what: Each hand is 5 rounds. Round 1 is the auction only: Bid, then Declare, so 2 choice steps. Rounds 2–5 are one trick each: Lead plus 3 Follows, so 4 choice steps.
changes.why: This keeps every round at 4 choice steps or fewer.
changes.fixes: Choice steps exceed the limit: the auction and declaration share a round with a full trick, giving 6 choice steps where at most 4 are allowed.

changes.what: Deal 4 cards to each player and leave 4 cards face down as a hidden talon that nobody sees. A hand therefore has 4 tricks, and 8 hands fill exactly 40 rounds.
changes.why: This keeps 8 hands, so each seat has priority twice and luck is diluted. The talon keeps uncertainty alive to the last trick.
changes.fixes: Moving the auction into its own round with 5 tricks per hand would allow only 4 hands in 40 rounds (6 rounds each). That gives one priority per seat and much more deal luck.

changes.what: The talon of 4 unseen cards also means no player can ever fully count the hands.
changes.why: Players must keep reasoning about where the top trumps and the called King are.
changes.fixes: With all 20 cards dealt, the hidden state collapses fast: by trick 3 a careful counter knows every hand, so late-hand inference is thin.

changes.what: There is a single unambiguous announcement rule. The trump suit and the call (a named King, or 'Solo') are announced to everyone. Only who holds the called King stays secret until the end of the hand.
changes.why: This removes the contradiction. Every player knows which cards are trumps.
changes.fixes: Rule 12 contradicts itself: trump is said to be both hidden and announced, so defenders cannot know which cards are trumps and following suit becomes unplayable.

changes.what: The Taker calls a King instead of a seat. Its holder becomes the concealed partner. If the Taker holds that King, or it lies in the talon, the Taker plays alone at partnership stakes.
changes.why: This restores the original's call mechanic. The Taker gets real uncertainty about the partner and the defenders get a real inference task.
changes.fixes: The partner is chosen by seat number, which loses the original's characteristic called King. It also lets the Taker pick a partner without any uncertainty about whether that partner is strong.

changes.what: Trick power is computed by a stated formula on the card code and the trump suit, not a per-card table.
changes.why: The engine has no lookup operation. A single calculation per card keeps the step count low.
changes.fixes: Choice steps exceed the limit: the auction and declaration share a round with a full trick, giving 6 choice steps where at most 4 are allowed.

keeps: Four players, an auction for the role of Taker, and the Taker naming trump.
The three permanent top trumps: Spadille (Ace of Spades) highest, Manille (the Two of trump), and Baste (Ace of Clubs).
Calling a King whose holder becomes a concealed partner, or playing solo against three.
Must follow suit, with trumping optional when you cannot follow.
Contracts are a majority of tricks for the Taker's side, solo pays double, and codille rewards the defender who beats a failed Taker.
Settlement by counters, a fresh deal every hand, and sides that change every hand.

recommendation.reason: The structure works. Splitting the auction into its own round, using 4-card hands with a hidden talon, and announcing trump publicly fixes the step count and the contradiction while keeping 8 hands.

variation.name: Petite Quadrille III
variation.summary: A four-player, 8-hand miniature of Quadrille played with a 20-card pack. Each hand begins with an auction round, followed by 4 tricks. Four cards lie unseen in a talon. The Taker names trump and calls a King whose holder is a secret partner, or goes solo. Spadille, Manille and Baste are the top trumps.
variation.rules:
CARDS
1. The pack has 20 cards. Each card's code is 10 × suit + rank.
   - Suits: Spades 1, Clubs 2, Hearts 3, Diamonds 4.
   - Ranks: Ace 1, Two 2, Jack 3, Queen 4, King 5.
   - Cards are shown as '<code> <Rank> of <Suit>', for example '35 King of Hearts'.
   - Code 11 (Ace of Spades) is Spadille. Code 21 (Ace of Clubs) is Baste. Both are always trumps.
2. Plain power (used only when a card is not a trump): King 5, Queen 4, Jack 3, Ace of Hearts or Diamonds 2, any Two 1. Codes 11 and 21 have plain power 0.

STRUCTURE
3. The game has 40 rounds, in 8 hands of 5 rounds. Hand h covers rounds 5h−4 to 5h. A round's position p (1 to 5) is its place in its hand.
4. Position 1 is the auction round, with no trick. Positions 2, 3, 4 and 5 each contain exactly one trick.
5. The priority seat of hand h is ((h − 1) mod 4) + 1. That is seats 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4, so each seat has priority twice.
6. Turn order always runs 1→2→3→4→1.
7. Whenever a player is asked to choose, they are first shown their current hand, the trump suit (once declared) and the call (once declared).

AUCTION ROUND (position 1)
8. Reset. Every player's hand_tricks becomes 0 and is_partner becomes false. The leader becomes the priority seat.
9. Deal. Shuffle the 20 cards. Deal 4 to each player privately and put the remaining 4 face down in the talon.
   - This is the round's only random draw.
   - Each player sees only their own 4 cards. Nobody ever sees the talon.
10. Bid. All four choose at the same moment, each picking one of: Pass, Assist, 3, 4.
   - Pass means no interest.
   - Assist signals willingness to be called. It does not compete for Taker.
   - 3 or 4 is an offer to be Taker with a contract of that many of the hand's 4 tricks for the Taker's side.
11. Resolve. Every bid is announced.
   - The highest numeric bid wins.
   - Between equal numeric bids, the winner is the first such seat in turn order starting from the priority seat.
   - If nobody bid a number, the priority seat becomes Taker with contract 3.
   - The Taker and the contract are announced.
12. Declare. The Taker alone chooses one of exactly 20 options:
   - a trump suit (Spades, Clubs, Hearts or Diamonds), combined with
   - either a called King (15 King of Spades, 25 King of Clubs, 35 King of Hearts, 45 King of Diamonds) or 'Solo'.
   - Options are labelled like 'Hearts, call 15 King of Spades' or 'Diamonds, Solo'.
13. Announcement. The trump suit t and the call (the named King, or 'Solo') are announced publicly to everyone. If a King was called:
   - If another player holds it, that player gets is_partner = true and is told privately 'You hold the called King: you are the Taker's partner.'
   - If the Taker holds it, or it is in the talon, the Taker plays alone but is NOT solo, and nobody is told this.
   - No one except the partner (and the Taker, if they hold the King) learns who the partner is until the end of the hand.

CARD STRENGTH (computed from code c and trump t, no table)
14. Effective suit: t if c is 11 or 21; otherwise floor(c / 10).
15. Trump power, for cards whose effective suit is t:
   - c = 11 (Spadille): 20.
   - c = 10t + 2 (Manille, the Two of trump): 19.
   - c = 21 (Baste): 18.
   - c = 10t + 1 when t is 3 or 4 (Ace of a red trump): 17.
   - Otherwise 11 + plain power, so King 16, Queen 15, Jack 14.
   - Every card whose effective suit is not t has trump power 0.

TRICK ROUNDS (positions 2 to 5)
16. Lead. The leader plays any card from their hand. It is removed at once. The led suit L is its effective suit.
17. Follow. The other three play one card each, in turn order after the leader. Each follower's offer is built from their current hand:
   - If they hold any card of effective suit L, the offer is exactly those cards.
   - Otherwise the offer is their whole hand, so they may trump or discard.
   - The played card is removed at once.
18. Winner. A card's trick power is:
   - its trump power, if above 0;
   - otherwise its plain power, if its effective suit is L;
   - otherwise 0.
   The highest trick power wins. Ties cannot occur among cards that can win.
19. The winner gains 1 hand_tricks and 1 tricks_won and leads the next trick. The four cards, who played each, and the winner are announced.

END OF HAND (after the trick at position 5)
20. Count.
   - The side's tricks are the Taker's hand_tricks, plus the partner's if a partner exists.
   - The contract is made if the side's tricks are at least the contract.
   - v = contract − 2, so 1 or 2.
21. Score.
   - With a partner, made: Taker +v, partner +v, each of the two defenders −v.
   - With a partner, failed: Taker −v, partner −v, each of the two defenders +v.
   - Alone by call (the called King was in the Taker's hand or the talon), made: Taker +v, each of the three defenders −v.
   - Alone by call, failed: Taker −v, each of the three defenders +v.
   - Solo, made: Taker +2v, each of the three defenders −v.
   - Solo, failed: Taker −2v, each of the three defenders +v.
22. Codille. If the contract failed and exactly one defender has more hand_tricks than the side's tricks, that defender scores an extra +1.
23. Reveal. The partner's seat (or 'alone' or 'solo'), the talon, each player's hand_tricks, the side's tricks and every score change are announced.

END OF GAME
24. After round 40 the game ends. Each player's standing is 100 × score + tricks_won.

There is no talk phase. The bid (including Assist) and the card play are the only signals.
variation.objective: After 40 rounds, the player with the highest score wins. If scores tie, the tied player with the most tricks_won wins (equivalently, the highest 100 × score + tricks_won). If that also ties, those players draw.
variation.expected_effect:
Every round now fits the 4-choice limit. Public trump removes the contradiction and makes following suit well defined. The hidden talon and the concealed King-holder create sustained inference:
- Defenders must read who the partner is, or whether the King sits in the talon.
- The Taker must judge whether the call will find a strong partner, or go solo for double stakes.
- Over 8 hands, bidding discipline beats overbidding and passivity.
- Codille punishes reckless Takers.
Talk stays out because sides are hidden and adversarial: open messages would be unverifiable partnership claims, and the bid already carries the Assist signal.

balanced.evidence:
SCORING ARITHMETIC. v = contract-1, so contract 3/4/5 gives v = 2/3/4. Every outcome sums to zero. Partnership: +v +v -v -v = 0. Solo: +3v -v -v -v = 0. Partnership is 2 against 2 and solo is 1 against 3, as labelled.

CARD COVERAGE. Trick powers cover every card.
- Trump Hearts or Diamonds (7 trumps): 11=20, Manille=19, 21=18, trump Ace=17, K=16, Q=15, J=14.
- Trump Spades or Clubs (6 trumps): the trump Ace is itself Spadille or Baste, so 17 is unused, as it should be.
- Non-trump led suit: K5, Q4, J3, red A2, Two 1. Black Aces are always trumps, so 'red Ace' is complete.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES (winner rule).
- Always bid 5 (last option). You become Taker on every hand where no one else bids 5, and win ties from priority. You must win 5/5 tricks. Your hand is random and your partner is chosen blind, so the side expects about 2.5 of 5 tricks before trump and Taker advantages. Taking all 5 is rare, roughly under 15%. Each failure costs -4 (partnership) or -12 (solo). Over 4 hands this policy finishes last against sensible play and usually against random play. It loses.
- Always Pass (first option). You are Taker only when all pass on your priority hand, at the forced contract 3. Otherwise your score is +-v, set by others' contracts and by whether you are blindly called as partner. Against sensible takers who only bid strong hands, defenders lose more often than they win. You are not protected, so this can lose.
- Always bid 3. When others pass you are Taker on weak hands and fail often at -2 each. Not dominant.
- Always solo. Payoff is +6 or -6 at contract 3 for 3 of 5 tricks against three. That is good only with strong trump holdings, so it is not dominant.
- Always play the first offered card. This throws away trick control and is beaten by sensible play.
- No bid or declaration is strictly better regardless of others. Over- and under-bidding both have costs.

SEATS. Priority (lead the first trick, win bid ties, forced Taker if all pass) rotates. Each seat holds it exactly once in 4 hands, so there is no structural seat edge. All four can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
RULES. The rules are complete and unambiguous, and the game is finite (24 rounds) and decided by arithmetic.
- Effective-suit, follow-suit and power rules cover every card and trump suit.
- Auction ties and the all-pass case are resolved.
- The 16 declaration options are explicit.
- Scoring and the tie-break (100 x score + tricks_won) are numeric.
- Hidden elements are hands and partner identity: 2 of 3 allowed.
- No board, judge or clock is needed. No trading or binding agreements.

TALK. No talk is the right call. Sides are hidden and adversarial, so free talk would only produce unverifiable claims about partnership. Card play is the intended signalling channel, as in real Quadrille.

COMPLEXITY LIMITS. The step list is flat, the same in every round, with `when` conditions. A round therefore has to carry every block, gated by `when`:
- Auction block: reset, deal, bid poll, resolve, declare poll, set partner/announce.
- Trick block: rebuild+lead, 3 x (rebuild+follow), power computation for 4 cards, winner and update.
- End-of-hand block: side tricks and contract check, scoring, announce.

CHOICE STEPS. The list then contains 6 choice steps (bid, declare, lead, follow x3), above the limit of 4. The designer's figure of 4 counts only the steps active in a given round.

TOTAL STEPS. The steps realistically exceed 20. Trick power alone has about 9 cases per card, and the engine has no lookup operation. The payoff_matrix workaround costs about 13 steps for 9 cells. The claimed 14 steps per round is not substantiated.

As specified, the declared complexity is unverified and very likely outside the limits.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
SAMPLE SIZE. There are only 4 deals of 5 cards each, with 5 tricks per hand. Follow-suit removes most play choices, leaving often 1 or 2 legal cards.

SWINGS. Score moves come in large lumps: +-2 to +-4 per hand, and up to +-12 for a solo. One strong deal, such as holding Spadille, Manille and Baste and making a solo, gives +6 to +12. That is usually enough to win the whole game. Over 4 deals there is no averaging.

PASSIVE EXPOSURE. Non-takers' results depend on being blindly named partner, which is chosen without card knowledge, and on others' bids.

ALL-GOOD-PLAY OUTCOME. If all four play well (bid strong hands only, sound declarations, good card play), the winner is mostly whoever was dealt the best hand or was luckily called as partner of a made contract.

ESTIMATE. Roughly 60-70% of the result is chance.

THERE IS REAL INFERENCE, but too little of it to overcome the deal:
- Reading bids.
- Deducing the hidden partner from play.
- Trump and partner choice.

required_changes: Reduce luck with duplicate dealing. Play 6 hands (36 rounds, within the limit of 40). In hands 2, 4 and 6, reuse the previous hand's 20-card deal, rotated so that each player receives the hand the player on their right held. Every strong holding is then played by another seat, and reasoning, not the deal, decides the winner.
Lower the solo multiplier from 3v to 2v for the Taker, or cap any single hand's swing. This stops one lucky solo from deciding the game.

Fit the flat step list within limits. Precompute trick power as a stored per-card attribute when trump is declared (one calc step per hand, not per trick). Merge the three follow polls by using a single sequential_choice step that loops over the three followers. Then the step list contains at most 4 choice steps (bid, declare, lead, follow) and at most 20 steps total, all gated by `when`. Restate steps_per_round and choice_steps_per_round as the full flat-list count.

balanced.evidence:
SCORE TABLE (v = contract − 2). Partnership made: Taker +v, partner +v, defenders −v each, so the sum is 0. Partnership failed: the reverse, plus codille +1 to at most one defender. Solo made: Taker +2v, three defenders −v each, so the sum is −v. Solo failed: Taker −2v, defenders +v each, so the sum is +v. The trick-taking incentives are consistent with the labels: making the contract is good for the Taker's side and bad for the defenders.

POLICIES UNDER THE WINNER RULE (highest score).
(a) Always bid 5. You win almost every auction, since a tie at 5 goes to the priority seat or the next seat in order. You then need all 5 of 5 tricks, against four 5-card hands drawn from 20 with up to 7 trumps out. Most hands fail at −3 (partner) or −6 (solo). Against sensible or random opponents this loses heavily.
(b) Always Pass. You are Taker only when you hold priority and nobody bids (contract 3, v = 1). Otherwise you always defend. Whenever opponents bid only good hands and make them, you lose v each time. It does not never-lose.
(c) Always Assist. This is the same as Pass, except that Takers may pick you as partner. You then share the outcome of a contract you did not size. It is not a guaranteed win.
(d) Always the first legal card, or always the last. This throws away high trumps or ducks winners at random relative to the trick. It loses to a player who counts cards: with 20 cards all dealt, every card is known to be held by someone.
(e) Always choose solo. Solo needs ≥3 tricks alone against 3 players. On ordinary hands this fails at −2v.
No option is strictly dominant: the bid depends on the hand, the partner choice depends on the Assist signals, and the card play depends on the trick.

SEAT EDGE. The priority seat breaks ties, is the default Taker and leads trick 1. Priority rotates 1, 2, 3, 4, 1, 2, 3, 4, so each seat holds every relative tie position exactly twice. Neither seat order nor information gives a structural edge.

CAN EVERYONE WIN? All four players are able to win. The game is zero-sum apart from the codille and solo asymmetries, which reward good judgment rather than a seat.

One note: the Taker can force any player to be partner, even one who passed. That player shares the result but cannot refuse. This is acceptable, because a Taker who picks badly also suffers.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
The deal is random each hand, and card luck matters: a hand holding Spadille, Manille and Baste is very strong. Skill has many levers against it, though.
- Bidding: sizing the contract to the hand, and passing with weak hands, limits the losses from bad deals.
- Partner choice: reading the Assist signals.
- Solo versus partner: weighing a payoff of 2v against needing 3 tricks alone.
- Card play: with all 20 cards dealt, the holdings are fully inferable as play proceeds. Players can count trumps, read the Assist bids, and infer the hidden partner from card play, which defenders must do to coordinate.

OUTCOME UNDER EQUAL GOOD PLAY. When all four play well, the results depend on who receives strong deals. Over 8 hands, with every seat bidding and defending, deal variance averages out partly but not fully. I estimate chance at about 40–50% of the result over 8 hands. That is similar to short-match bridge or whist, where a stronger player is clearly favoured over a weaker one.

The winner is not decided by a single draw. There is real hidden information (hands, partner identity) and real ways to act on it (bids, partner choice, leads, ducking).

Caveat: if the playable fix reduces the number of hands, the chance share rises, so keep as many hands as the limits allow.

required_changes: Playable: fix rule 12's contradiction. Announce the trump suit publicly, keep only the partner identity and solo status hidden until the end of the hand, and state this in a single unambiguous sentence.

Playable: bring choice steps to 4 or fewer per round. For example, move the auction into its own round: each hand becomes 6 rounds, with position 0 holding Reset, Deal, Bid and Declare, and positions 1–5 holding one trick each. To stay within 40 rounds and keep priority equal, use 4 hands × 6 = 24 rounds, with each seat taking priority once. Alternatively, keep 40 rounds by removing the separate Declare choice: fold trump and partner into the bid poll, where the winning bidder's pre-committed trump and partner apply. Update the stated complexity to the true counts in either case.

balanced.evidence:
SCORING TABLE per hand (v = contract-2): partner made T+v, P+v, D-v, D-v (sum 0); partner failed is the reverse; alone-by-call made T+v, D-v x3; solo made T+2v, D-v x3; failures reverse these; codille adds +1 to one defender. The labels match the numbers. Solo doubles both the gain and the loss of an alone taker, but it is announced publicly. Calling your own King or a talon King keeps the defenders guessing at half the stake. Neither option dominates the other.

THOUGHTLESS POLICIES under the winner rule (highest final score):
(a) Always bid 4. You win the auction almost every hand: ties go by priority order, and you beat all bids of 3. The side then needs all 4 tricks, with 8 of 16 dealt cards against 8. That is roughly 15-25% even with a good call. EV is about p*2-(1-p)*2, roughly -1.2 per hand as taker, so this policy loses against sensible play and against random play.
(b) Always Pass. You are only Taker when forced (all pass, you have priority, contract 3). Otherwise you defend contracts that sensible bidders chose because their hands were strong, where the make rate is above 50% and defender EV is slightly negative. You never take the +v/+2v swings, so you trail a competent opponent but can beat a random bidder. You do not win or draw almost always.
(c) Always bid 3. You are Taker whenever nobody bids 4 and you are first in priority order among the 3s, including with weak hands. Calls with weak 4-card hands fail often, so this loses to selective bidders.
(d) First option in card play, or a fixed declaration such as 'Spades, call 15 King of Spades'. Leading or following blindly concedes tricks, and a fixed trump ignores the hand.

No policy wins or draws every time, and no bid or declaration is strictly better regardless of opponents. Assist has no mechanical effect, only a signal, so it is not dominant either.

SEATS: priority (forced taker, bid tie-breaks, first lead) rotates 1,2,3,4,1,2,3,4, so each seat holds it twice. Seat 4 has priority in the last hand, with full knowledge of the standings, which is a small edge. The tiebreak tricks_won is at most 32, so 100*score+tricks_won equals score-first ordering. All four players can realistically win.

playable.evidence:
LIMITS: Steps, counted with `when`-gated steps in one flat list: auction reset, deal, bid poll, resolve, declare, announce/partner = 6; trick lead, 3 follows, winner = 5; end of hand count/score, codille, reveal = 3 or more. That is about 14-16 against a stated 12, still within 20. Choice steps per round: auction has 2 (bid poll, declare), trick has 4 (lead plus 3 follows), so at most 4. Rounds 40, random draws 1 per round (the deal), attributes about 18. Hidden elements are the private hands, the talon and the partner identity. That is 3, not the stated 2, but still within the limit of 3. Card strength is computed by formula (rules 14-18) with no lookup. I checked tie-freedom: trump powers are 20/19/18/17/16/15/14, and led-suit plain powers are K5 Q4 J3 A2 2-1 with no duplicates. Bid ties, the all-pass case and every call case are defined. The game is finite and decided by arithmetic on numbers the game keeps.

TALK: correctly omitted. This is hidden-partner trick-taking, and the bids, Assist and card play are the intended signals. Free talk would let the partner announce themselves, removing the inference. The bid is a simultaneous poll, which is correct.

GAP that fails the check: rules 16-17 remove each played card 'at once' but never announce it. Rule 7 shows a chooser only their hand, the trump and the call. Only rule 19 reveals the four cards, after the trick. So a follower is not told the led card. A void follower is not even told the led suit L. Nobody sees which cards were already played to the current trick. That makes the central trick decisions (trump or discard, overtake a partner or not) unplayable as written. Rule 7 also omits the Taker, the contract and the bids from the shown information, although rule 11 announces them.

reasoning_over_luck.evidence:
There is real material to infer. The partner is hidden, and the Taker may even be secretly alone. Assist bids signal willingness to be called, played cards reveal suits, and the talon is unseen. Players must decide whether to bid 3 or 4 or pass, which of 20 trump/call combinations to declare, Solo versus a concealed alone, whom to treat as partner, and when to trump. Each decision can act on these inferences.

Chance is substantial. Only 8 deals occur, and 4-card hands give few card-play choices. Following suit is often forced, and on average each player is Taker about twice. I estimate 45-55% of the result is chance.

Under equal good play, outcomes do depend on the deals. However, skill moves the result in every hand: avoiding hopeless 4-bids, picking the call, misdirecting with a concealed alone, and placing the partner correctly from Assist and the play. A strong player clearly beats a weak or random one over 8 hands, and a bad deal can be offset by declining to bid and by sound defence. The deal is not the sole decider.
reasoning_over_luck.notes: Pass, though the luck share is high.

required_changes: Playable: announce each card publicly the moment it is played in rules 16-17 ('Seat X plays <card>'). Extend rule 7 so every chooser is shown: the Taker's seat, the contract, all announced bids, the led suit L and the cards already played to the current trick (with seats), and the completed tricks of the current hand.

Playable: correct the stated complexity to hidden_elements 3 (hands, talon, partner identity) and steps_per_round about 15 (auction, trick and end-of-hand steps share one flat when-gated list), so the declared figures match the design.
